formation.title: Two Kings, One People
formation.text:
Gowa and Bone answer to one court now, and the court sits again at Gowa, between the old royal hill of Kale Gowa and the beach where Somba Opu would rise. For two centuries the peninsula lived by oaths: the nine banners of Gowa took a king descended from heaven on their own terms, Gowa and Talloq swore that they were two kings and one people, and the Bugis kingdoms of Bone, Wajo and Soppeng bound themselves into the alliance of the three powers to keep any one crown from mastering them all.

Now one crown has. The question is what it will do with the peninsula. The Talloq way is the way of the chancellors: share the crown with a council of able men, keep the custom that each land chooses its own lord, and open the harbour to every ship that comes, Malay, Chinese, Portuguese or English. The Gowa way is the way of the sword: one court, one law, the corvee of the conquered lands put to walls and canals, and the Bugis lords taught that the custom of the peninsula is whatever Gowa says it is.

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Two kings, one people: the chancellors keep the open port

modifiers.name: Two Kings, One People
modifiers.text: The dual state of Gowa and Talloq: the chancellors govern, the harbour is open to every nation, and the crown shares its power.

options.text: One crown over the south: Gowa's sword makes one kingdom

modifiers.name: One Crown over the South
modifiers.text: Gowa's sword makes one kingdom of the peninsula, and the lords of the banners and the Bugis kingdoms learn to obey.

advances.name: Compact of the Tumanurung
advances.text: Gowa's first ruler was a tumanurung, one who descended from heaven, and the heads of the nine banners, the Bate Salapang, accepted her on terms: they kept their lands, their customs and the right to choose her successors. The nobles of Gowa never forgot that the crown was theirs to give.

advances.name: Iron of Luwu
advances.text: Luwu, eldest of the kingdoms of the peninsula, mined iron in the hills around Lake Matano and sold it across the Java Sea, where the keris smiths prized it for the pale pattern it gave their blades.

advances.name: Tubarani Retinues
advances.text: Every lord of the peninsula kept his tubarani, the brave ones: men bound to him by debt, birth or oath, who carried kris, spear and shield wherever he went and fought to defend his honour, his siri'.

advances.name: The Lontaraq Script
advances.text: The Bugis and Makassarese wrote their own languages in their own script, on long strips of palm leaf wound on spools: genealogies, treaties, law books and the cantos of their epic.

advances.name: Buffalo and Plough
advances.text: From about 1300 the stock-handle plough and the water buffalo turned the marshy plains of Maros and the Jeneberang into bunded wet fields, and rice became the food of the peninsula and the wealth of its lords.

advances.name: Bissu of the Arajang
advances.text: The bissu, priests who stand between man and woman and between earth and heaven, guard the arajang, the sacred regalia in which the sovereignty of each kingdom resides, and speak the language of the gods at every royal rite.

advances.name: I La Galigo
advances.text: The adventures of Sawerigading, prince of Luwu, and his son I La Galigo fill the longest epic of the archipelago, recited by the bissu and copied by scribes in every Bugis court.

advances.name: Outriggers of Mandar
advances.text: The Mandar sailors of Balanipa built narrow outriggers under a single great sail, the fastest boats on the coasts of Sulawesi, for fishing, courier work and the quick raid.

advances.name: The Blowpipe Makers
advances.text: The blowpipe and the poisoned dart were the weapons of the forest villages and the hill country, and the blowpipe makers were among the crafts the kings of Gowa called to their service.

advances.name: Ports of the Nagarakretagama
advances.text: The court poem of Majapahit, written in 1365, names Bantayan, Luwuk, Makasar and Salaya among the lands of its tribute. Chinese and Vietnamese ceramics of the age fill the graves of the peninsula's chiefs.

advances.name: Talloq, Kingdom of the Sea
advances.text: Late in the fifteenth century Karaeng Loe ri Sero, beaten in a quarrel over the throne of Gowa, went down to the coast and founded Talloq: a kingdom of harbours, boats and traders from its first day.

advances.name: Rua Karaeng Se're Ata
advances.text: Two kings, one people: the oath that bound Gowa and Talloq under Tumapa'risi Kallonna and was never broken without, so the chronicles say, the curse of God on the oathbreaker. The twin kingdom grew by such contracts and marriages more than by conquest.

advances.name: The Sabannaraq
advances.text: Tumapa'risi Kallonna created the office of sabannaraq, the harbourmaster, and gave it first to Daeng Pamatteq: one man to take the king's dues and speak for every foreign trader in the port.

advances.name: Written Law and Written War
advances.text: The chronicle of Gowa credits Tumapa'risi Kallonna with the first written laws of the kingdom, and with the first wars declared in writing.

advances.name: The Ramparts of Kale Gowa
advances.text: Earthen walls rose around the royal hill of Kale Gowa in the reign of Tumapa'risi Kallonna, a generation before his son learned to fire bricks.

advances.name: Tunipalangga's Bricks
advances.text: King Tunipalangga, 1546 to 1565, was the first to make bricks, the first to raise brick walls around the forts, the first to make gunpowder and the first to lay heavy corvee on his people. His great work was Somba Opu.

event.title: The Walls of Somba Opu
event.text: The chronicle of Gowa lists the deeds of King Tunipalangga as a craftsman would list his tools: he was the first to make bricks, the first to raise brick walls around the great forts, the first to make gunpowder, and the first to lay heavy corvee on his people. All four meet at Somba Opu, the citadel at the mouth of the Jeneberang. Its walls of fired brick, thick enough to carry cannon, will shelter the court, the arsenal and the royal storehouses for a hundred years, until the Dutch and the Bugis of Arung Palakka bring them down in June 1669 after one of the hardest sieges the Company ever fought in the Indies.

options.text: Let the brickmakers fire their kilns

modifiers.name: The Walls of Somba Opu
modifiers.text: Fired brick, gunpowder and the corvee of the whole kingdom raise the citadel of the kings.

advances.name: The Masters of the Crafts
advances.text: Tunipalangga set officials, the tu makkajannangngang, over the crafts of the kingdom: blacksmiths, goldsmiths, house builders, boat builders, blowpipe makers, copper workers and ropemakers, each answerable to the king.

advances.name: The Compact with the Malays
advances.text: In 1561 Tunipalangga swore a pact with Datuk Maharaja Bonang that let the Malay merchants settle in Makassar for good, and gave the market standard weights and scales. His successor built them the Katangka mosque while his own court still kept the old gods.

advances.name: Musu' Selleng
advances.text: The war of Islam, 1608 to 1611: having accepted the faith, the twin kingdom offered it to the Bugis and then imposed it, on Soppeng, on Wajo and at last on Bone.

event.title: Musu' Selleng
event.text:
In September 1605 Karaeng Matoaya of Talloq, chancellor of the twin kingdom, recited the confession of faith before Dato ri Bandang of Minangkabau and took the name Sultan Abdullah; the young king of Gowa followed him as Sultan Alauddin, and within two years the court and its people had followed both. Then the kings sent word to the Bugis that they had found a good new thing and offered to share it. Soppeng refused and was conquered in 1609, Wajo in 1610, Bone in 1611. This was Musu' Selleng, the war of Islam.

Yet the peace that followed was strangely mild. Every Bugis kingdom kept its own king, its own regalia and its own customary law, in return for a nominal acceptance of the faith. Was the sword the point, or the settlement?

options.text: Carry the faith further, by the sword if need be

modifiers.name: The Sword of the Faith
modifiers.text: The war of Islam goes on beyond the Bugis lands.

options.text: Leave each kingdom its king and its custom

modifiers.name: The Mild Settlement
modifiers.text: Each conquered kingdom keeps its king, its regalia and its customary law, and accepts the faith in name.

advances.name: The Open Sea
advances.text: "God made the land and the sea; the land he divided among men and the sea he gave in common." Sultan Alauddin's answer to the Dutch made Makassar the harbour of everyone the Company wished to shut out.

event.title: God Made the Land and the Sea
event.text:
The Dutch factors are back at the palace, as they have been every year since they opened their lodge in 1607, and their demand has not changed: close the port to the Portuguese and sell the cloves of the Moluccas to the Company alone. Sultan Alauddin's answer is copied into their letters home: "God made the land and the sea; the land he divided among men and the sea he gave in common. It has never been heard that anyone should be forbidden to sail the seas."

The English came in 1613 and the Danes in 1618, the French from Saint Malo in 1622 and Chinese junks from 1619. The English have begun to bring muskets, powder and Indian cloth in quantity, and they would like to be more than one nation among many.

options.text: My country stands open to all nations

modifiers.name: Open to All Nations
modifiers.text: The sea was given in common, and Makassar's harbour stands open to every ship that comes.

options.text: Make the English the armourers of Makassar

modifiers.name: The English Arms Trade
modifiers.text: English ships bring muskets, powder and Indian cloth to the arsenal of the kings.

advances.name: The Fleet of Swift Galleys
advances.text: Under Karaeng Matoaya and Sultan Alauddin the kingdom built a navy of swift galleys and sailing ships, rowed by the corvee of the conquered lands, that carried its armies to Sumbawa, Buton, Lombok and the Moluccas.

advances.name: Guns, Armour and Long Swords
advances.text: The chronicle notes that the short reign of Tunipasuluq, 1590 to 1593, saw the first use in war of guns, armour and long swords. The fighting men of Makassar never went back to the shield and the spear alone.

advances.name: Pattingalloang's Globe
advances.text: Karaeng Pattingalloang, chancellor from 1639 to 1654, read Portuguese, Spanish and Latin, bought a Galilean telescope and ordered from Amsterdam one of the largest globes ever made.

event.title: The Chancellor's Globe
event.text: Karaeng Pattingalloang, chancellor since 1639, does not ask the foreign merchants for strange animals or rich cloths. He asks for books, maps, a Galilean telescope from England, and in 1644 he sends sandalwood to Batavia to pay for a globe from the best mapmakers of Amsterdam, one of the largest ever made. The Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes found him reading European histories and working at mathematics day and night, and even the Company's men called him a man of great knowledge, science and understanding. Under him the court has gunnery manuals translated from Spanish, Portuguese and Turkish, keeps a diary of its own doings, and writes chronicles that record the failures of kings as well as their triumphs.

options.text: Set the globe in the chancellor's hall

modifiers.name: The Chancellor's Library
modifiers.text: Books in Portuguese, Spanish and Latin, a telescope and a great globe at the court of Makassar.

advances.name: Treatises on Gunnery
advances.text: The court of Makassar had manuals of gunnery translated into Makassarese from Spanish, Portuguese, Turkish and Malay, and cast its guns by them.

advances.name: The Custom of Passempe
advances.text: After Bone was beaten at Passempe in 1644, Pattingalloang held to the custom of the peninsula: the victor does not choose the king of the vanquished.

event.title: The Custom of Passempe
event.text:
Bone has risen and been beaten again, at Passempe in 1644, and its king has fled. The lords of the court want a Makassarese prince on the throne of Bone. The chancellor Pattingalloang will not hear of it: "It is the custom that if we choose a raja, the Bone people are not involved, and if Bone chooses a raja, we in turn are not involved."

The custom has served the twin kingdom well. It will not stop a later king from sending ten thousand men of Bone to dig the canal of the Jeneberang, and the memory of that humiliation will follow a young prince of Bone named Arung Palakka all the way to Batavia.

options.text: Keep the custom: Bone chooses its own king

modifiers.name: The Custom of the Two Crowns
modifiers.text: The victor does not choose the king of the vanquished: each land keeps its own lord.

options.text: Rule Bone from Somba Opu

modifiers.name: Ruled from Somba Opu
modifiers.text: Bone answers to the court at Gowa, and its men dig the king's canal.

advances.name: The Sons of Angke
advances.text: Arung Palakka's Bugis followers, settled in exile on the Angke river outside Batavia, fought for the Company in Sumatra, Buton and at last at Makassar, and were counted the best native soldiers of the Indies.

advances.name: The Code of Amanna Gappa
advances.text: The Wajorese merchants of Makassar wrote down the law of their trade under their headman La Pataello, called Amanna Gappa: cargo and freight shares, debts, the duties of captain and crew, and the fee for every port from Aceh to Manila.

advances.name: The Panrita Lopi
advances.text: The master boatbuilders of Ara, Lemo-Lemo and Tanaberu built their hulls on the open beach without plans, plank by plank, with rites at every stage from the felling of the keel tree to the launch.

advances.name: The Voyage to Marege
advances.text: Every monsoon the trepang fleets of Makassar sailed for Marege, the coast of Arnhem Land, to gather and cure sea cucumber for the Chinese market.

event.title: The Voyage to Marege
event.text: When the northwest monsoon sets in each December, the padewakang leave Makassar in their dozens, a thousand men aboard, and run east and south past Timor to a coast they call Marege. There they spend the dry months diving for trepang along the reefs, boiling it, drying it and smoking it in camps ashore, trading cloth, knives and tobacco with the Yolngu of the coast, and sail home on the southeast wind with cargoes for the Chinese junks. The Yolngu will remember the Macassans in their songs, their words and their kin for generations after the last fleet sails.

options.text: Fill the holds for the junks

modifiers.name: The Trepang Fleets
modifiers.text: Every monsoon the fleets sail for Marege and come home laden for the Chinese junks.

advances.name: The Pinisi
advances.text: The Bugis shipwrights took the gaff sails of European schooners onto their own hulls and made the pinisi, the ship that carried the trade of the archipelago into the age of steam.

advances.name: The Daeng Kingmakers
advances.text: Five Bugis brothers, sons of a prince of Luwu, put Sultan Sulaiman on the throne of Johor in 1722 and held the office of Yang Dipertuan Muda of Riau after him. Their kin founded the sultanate of Selangor.

advances.name: La Maddukelleng
advances.text: La Maddukelleng came home from exile in Pasir in the 1730s, was raised Arung Matoa by the elected council of Wajo, and carried the war against the Company to the walls of Makassar itself.

advances.name: Raja Haji Fisabilillah
advances.text: Raja Haji, Bugis Yang Dipertuan Muda of Riau, led his fleet against Dutch Malacca in 1784 and fell at Teluk Ketapang, remembered ever after as the warrior in the path of God.

destiny.name: The Peninsula under One Court
destiny.text: Gowa and Bone answer to one court, and the question the formation answered is now a road to walk. Keep the realm stable, and the destiny of Makassar opens: the free port of the chancellors, or the crown of Gowa over the islands.

conditions.text: Stability at least 25

event.title: The Peninsula under One Court
event.text: The heralds have carried the news to every banner of Gowa, to the lords of Bone and Wajo and Soppeng, to Luwu and to the Mandar coast: the peninsula answers to one court. The old alliances that kept any one crown from mastering the rest are spent. What remains to be decided is whether the new kingdom will look to its harbour or to its fleets, and the court has already chosen.

options.text: Let the drums of the court sound

destiny.name: The Harbour of the Sabannaraq
destiny.text: Tumapa'risi Kallonna gave the harbour of Makassar one master, the sabannaraq, to take the king's dues and speak for every foreign trader, and Tunipalangga gave its market standard weights and scales. Build the Office of the Sabannaraq at Gowa, grow Gowa by a quarter from its starting development to 25, and hold 1000 gold.

conditions.text: Chose the Two Kings, One People destiny.
The Office of the Sabannaraq stands at Gowa, and Gowa is ours
Gowa is ours and has development of at least 25
Gold at least 1000
Stability at least 25

event.title: The Harbourmaster's Port
event.text: The sabannaraq sits in his office by the beach, and the traders come to him: Malays from Johor and Patani, Javanese with rice and cloth, Chinese masters asking for trepang and tortoiseshell. He takes the king's dues by the king's weights and settles their quarrels by the king's law. A foreign merchant in Makassar has one man to answer to and one man to speak for him, and the word has gone round every harbour of the archipelago.

options.text: Let every ship find its spokesman here

destiny.name: The Free Sea
destiny.text: "The sea he gave in common." While the Company closed the Moluccas, the cloves of Hitu and Hoamoal came to Makassar, and the English, Danes and Portuguese kept their lodges on its beach. Raise the Foreign Lodges in two ports, hold Pasir on the Borneo coast, where the Wajorese merchants made a second home, grow Gowa by half to development 30, and hold 2000 gold.

conditions.text: The Foreign Lodges stand in at least 2 of our locations
Own Paser, or a subject owns it
Gowa is ours and has development of at least 30
Gold at least 2000
Stability at least 25

event.title: The Free Sea
event.text:
The Company has closed Ambon and Banda and burns the clove trees it cannot guard, yet the cloves still come to Makassar: the chiefs of Hitu and Hoamoal sell to Makassarese traders what they will not sell to Batavia, and the English, Danes and Portuguese buy them on the beach. In 1641 Malacca falls to the Company, and the Portuguese who will not live under it bring their families, their priests and their money to Makassar.

The Dutch call it smuggling. The court calls it the sea that God gave in common. How shall the free port spend its good fortune?

options.text: Buy every clove the Company cannot

modifiers.name: The Clove Trade of the Free Port
modifiers.text: The cloves of Hitu and Hoamoal come to Makassar in defiance of the Company. The port's wealth is in its holds, not its walls.

options.text: Give the Portuguese of Malacca a home

modifiers.name: Refuge of the Malacca Portuguese
modifiers.text: The Portuguese driven from Malacca in 1641 settle in Makassar with their families, their priests and their capital.

effects.name: Possible Burghers in Towns and Cities

destiny.name: The Chancellor's Kingdom
destiny.text: Under Matoaya and Pattingalloang, Talloq's chancellors governed the twin kingdom with books, letters and the custom that every land keeps its own king. Make Gowa a city, build Pattingalloang's Library, keep at least two subject kings under the crown, and hold 3000 gold and 75 prestige.

conditions.text: Gowa is ours and has grown into a city
Pattingalloang's Library stands in one of our locations
We have at least 2 subjects
Gold at least 3000
Prestige at least 75
Stability at least 25

event.title: The Chancellor's Kingdom
event.text:
Makassar is a city of many nations now, and the chancellor governs it the way Matoaya and Pattingalloang did: from a hall full of books and letters, with a diary of the court kept day by day, and with the custom that every land under the twin crown keeps its own king. Envoys come and go to Manila and Goa, to Macau and Batavia, to Mataram and Golconda. The Jesuits and the Company's men alike write home that they have met a man of great learning.

The chancellery cannot do everything at once. Shall it look inward to the government of the realm, or outward to the courts of the east?

options.text: Keep the diary of the court, day by day

modifiers.name: The Diary of the Court
modifiers.text: The chancellery of Gowa and Talloq records the doings of the court day by day, and governs by the record.

options.text: Send envoys to every court of the east

modifiers.name: Envoys to Every Court
modifiers.text: Letters and envoys go from Makassar to Manila, Goa, Macau, Batavia, Mataram and Golconda. The court of the pen neglects the sword.

destiny.name: Over the Water to Sumbawa
destiny.text: Once the Bugis kingdoms had accepted the faith, Gowa's fleets turned south across the Flores Sea. Sumbawa was invaded in 1618 and its rulers were made to convert and to own Gowa as their overlord. Hold Bima, Dompu and Sumbawa, yourself or through your subjects.

conditions.text: Chose the One Crown over the South destiny.
Own Bima, or a subject owns it
Own Dompu, or a subject owns it
Own Sumbawa, or a subject owns it
Stability at least 25

event.title: Over the Water to Sumbawa
event.text: The galleys of Gowa have crossed the Flores Sea. Bima, Dompu and Sumbawa have bowed, their rulers have recited the confession of faith, and their princes will marry into the royal house of Gowa. The horses of Dompu and the rice of Bima now feed the court at Somba Opu, and the captains are already asking which coast comes next.

options.text: Sumbawa is ours, and the sea beyond it

destiny.name: Ternate's Islands
destiny.text: From the open war of 1615 and 1616, Gowa and Ternate, the Company's ally, fought over the islands between them. Hold Buton and Banggai, build the citadel of Somba Opu, and hold 50 prestige.

conditions.text: Own Butung, or a subject owns it
Own Banggai, or a subject owns it
Somba Opu stands in one of our locations
Prestige at least 50
Stability at least 25

event.title: Ternate's Islands
event.text:
For half a century Gowa and Ternate have fought over the islands between them, and the Company has stood behind Ternate since the open war of 1615. Now Buton and Banggai fly Gowa's banners. Buton was always the hardest: the great fleet Gowa sent against it in 1666 was lost there to the Company and to Arung Palakka's Bugis.

The captains want walls on the islands. The court wants their tribute and their princes as hostages at Somba Opu.

options.text: Wall the islands and hold them

modifiers.name: Garrisons of the Islands
modifiers.text: Walls and garrisons hold the islands taken from Ternate's sultan.

options.text: Take tribute and hostages and sail home

modifiers.name: Tribute and Hostages
modifiers.text: The islands pay in goods and in princes, and the corvee for the wars takes men from the workshops.

destiny.name: Master of the Eastern Seas
destiny.text: At its height Gowa's word ran from Lombok to the islands of Ternate's sultan, but Ternate itself never fell to it. Hold the whole of Lombok and Ternate, and 75 prestige: what Gowa reached for and never held.

conditions.text: Own Sasak, or a subject owns it
Own Lombok, or a subject owns it
Own Ternate, or a subject owns it
Prestige at least 75
Stability at least 25

event.title: Master of the Eastern Seas
event.text: Lombok is Gowa's from shore to shore, and the banner of the twin kingdom flies over Ternate, the city whose sultans and their Dutch friends held the clove islands against Makassar for half a century. No king of Gowa ever stood here. From Selayar to the Moluccas the sea lanes answer to one court, and the vassal kings of a dozen islands send their envoys to Somba Opu.

options.text: Keep the galley fleets at sea

modifiers.name: Galleys of the Eastern Seas
modifiers.text: The war galleys of Gowa keep the sea lanes from Selayar to the Moluccas.

options.text: Call the vassal kings to war

modifiers.name: The Vassal Kings March
modifiers.text: The kings under Gowa's crown bring their men to its wars and share in its victories.

units.name: Tubarani
units.text: The brave ones: retainers of the karaeng and of the nine banners, with kris, spear and shield.

units.name: Pasumpi
units.text: Blowpipe men of the villages and hills, whose poisoned darts struck from cover.

units.name: Kalewang Swordsmen
units.text: Fighting men in chain shirts with the long kalewang blade, the heavy foot of the kings of Makassar.

units.name: To Angke
units.text: Bugis musket and spear men in the tradition of Arung Palakka's exiles: fast, bold and feared across the Indies.

units.name: Sandeq
units.text: The narrow Mandar outrigger with its single great sail: the fastest boat on the coast, built to scout and carry word rather than to fight in line.

units.name: Karaeng's War Galley
units.text: The long oared galleys of the kings of Makassar, crowded with boarding parties and rowed by the corvee of the conquered lands.

units.name: Makassar Bronze Guns
units.text: Heavy bronze guns cast and served by the rules of translated European and Turkish manuals: hard hitting, slow to drag.

units.name: Padewakang
units.text: The broad two-masted trader of the Wajorese merchants and the trepang fleets, with room for cargo and crew on long monsoon passages.

units.name: Pinisi
units.text: The Bugis schooner of Ara and Lemo-Lemo: fast, seaworthy and lightly armed, built for trade more than for battle.

buildings.name: Tana Sawah
buildings.text: Bunded wet fields of the plains, worked with buffalo and plough, that feed the towns and fill the ships.

buildings.name: Earthen Ramparts
buildings.text: A ring of earthen walls around a royal seat, in the manner of Kale Gowa.

buildings.name: Office of the Sabannaraq
buildings.text: The harbourmaster's house, where the king's dues are taken and every foreign trader finds his spokesman.

buildings.name: Somba Opu
buildings.text: The brick citadel of the kings at the mouth of the Jeneberang, with the court, the arsenal and the royal storehouses inside its walls.

effect_groups.label: To the country, when built in the capital

buildings.name: Forge of the Panre Bessi
buildings.text: The smiths and goldsmiths the king's guild masters call to his service, working the iron of Luwu and the gold of the islands.

buildings.name: The Foreign Lodges
buildings.text: The factories of the English, Danes and Portuguese and the quarters of the Malays and Chinese along the beach of the city.

buildings.name: Pattingalloang's Library
buildings.text: The chancellor's hall of books, atlases and instruments, with a globe from Amsterdam and a telescope from England.

effect_groups.label: To the country, when built in the capital

buildings.name: Yards of the Panrita Lopi
buildings.text: Beach yards where the master boatbuilders raise their hulls plank by plank.

buildings.name: Trepang Station
buildings.text: A camp of boiling pans and smokehouses where sea cucumber is cured for the Chinese market. With the pans ashore the divers can take all the reef gives before the catch spoils, and the fishery off its coast lands more.

where.text: The location's raw material is Fish

list.name: The Tumabicarabutta
list.text: The tumabicarabutta, he who speaks for the land, is the chancellor of Gowa, and the office belongs to the ruler of Talloq. The first, Tumamenang ri Makkoayang, took charge of the kingdom's defence, its diplomacy and the education of its princes. Karaeng Matoaya held it from 1590 and was the most powerful man in South Sulawesi: he crowned King Tunipasuluq and deposed him in 1593. Karaeng Pattingalloang, chancellor from 1639 to 1654, read Portuguese, Spanish and Latin and filled the court with the instruments of European learning.

list.name: The Bate Salapang
list.text: The Nine Banners: the heads of the nine communities of Gowa, who swore allegiance to Karaeng Bayo and the tumanurung descended from heaven in return for their traditional rights. They sit as the council of customary law, and no king is installed without them. Their men march under the nine banners, and the first sabannaraq, Daeng Pamatteq, commanded them for the king.

conditions.text: Owns Gowa

list.name: The Tumailalang
list.text: King Tunipalangga, 1546 to 1565, gave the harbourmaster's duties outside the port to a new minister of the interior, the tumailalang, who runs the daily affairs of the kingdom and carries word between the court and the council of the nine banners. Under Tunijalloq there were two, the elder and the younger. Prominent commoners held the office at first; in later reigns it went to karaeng.

list.name: The Parewa Sara'
list.text: Talloq's ruler accepted Islam on 22 September 1605, taught by the Minangkabau scholar Datuk ri Bandang, and the first Friday prayer was held at Talloq in 1607. The sara', the law of Islam, was joined to the four pillars of the adat as the fifth, with its own officials: a kadi above, and imams and khatibs at the mosques who marry, bury and divide inheritances, paid from the zakat. From 1630 they were drawn from the nobility.

conditions.text: Islam group
